title: Deathtouch and trample
answer: Yes. With deathtouch, any nonzero damage counts as lethal, so you assign just 1 damage to each blocker and the rest tramples over to the player (or planeswalker or battle) it's attacking.
coach: Put deathtouch and trample on your biggest attacker: each blocker only soaks 1 damage, so chump blocks barely help your opponent.

formats.commander: Same rule. In multiplayer the extra damage goes to the player, planeswalker or battle that creature is attacking, and combat damage from a commander also counts toward 21 commander damage.
formats.brawl: Same rule. Brawl doesn't use the 21 commander damage rule, so only the life loss matters.

title: Responding to a land
answer: No one can respond to a land being played. Playing a land is a special action that doesn't use the stack. Any abilities it triggers (like landfall) do use the stack, and those can be responded to.
coach: Respond to the landfall trigger instead, or plan to answer the land on your own turn.

formats.commander: Same rule. Every opponent can respond to a landfall trigger, one at a time in turn order.

title: Mana abilities
answer: Mana abilities don't use the stack, so they resolve immediately and can't be responded to. You can activate them whenever you have priority or while paying a cost.
coach: Tap for mana as late as possible; mana you make empties at the end of each step.

formats.commander: Same rule.

title: An object leaves before its ability resolves
answer: Usually the ability still works. If an effect needs information about an object that has left the zone it was expected to be in, it uses that object's last known information. The exception is when the ability targets that object: a target that changed zones is illegal (see the targets rule).
coach: Graveyard removal in response usually doesn't stop the effect; to stop it, counter the ability itself or remove the card before the trigger happens.

formats.commander: Same rule. If your commander goes to the command zone in response, the ability still uses its last known information.
formats.brawl: Same rule, including for your commander.

title: Targets that become illegal
answer: A spell or ability checks its targets as it resolves. If every target is illegal, it doesn't resolve (it 'fizzles'). If only some are illegal, it resolves and does as much as it can to the legal ones.
coach: To 'fizzle' an opponent's removal, give your creature hexproof or protection, or remove it yourself in response; the spell then does nothing.

formats.commander: Same rule. If a targeted commander is moved to the command zone in response, it's an illegal target and that spell or ability can't affect it.
formats.brawl: Same rule, including for your commander.

title: Summoning sickness
answer: A creature that hasn't been under your control since your turn began can't attack or use its own abilities with {T} or {Q} in the cost, unless it has haste. It can still be tapped to pay costs of other permanents' abilities, such as crew, station or convoke.
coach: New creatures can't attack, but they can still crew, station or convoke the turn they arrive, so play them before you need those costs.

formats.commander: Same rule. A commander that's cast again from the command zone is a new object and is summoning sick again.
formats.brawl: Same rule, including for a recast commander.

title: Station
answer: Station taps another untapped creature you control and puts charge counters on the Spacecraft or Planet equal to that creature's power, at sorcery speed. A creature that just arrived can be used, because station is the Spacecraft's ability, not the creature's own {T} ability.
coach: Station with creatures that can't attack well anyway (or just arrived), and do it in your main phase before combat.

formats.commander: Same rule. A Spacecraft with a power/toughness box can be your commander (CR 903.3).
formats.brawl: Same rule. A Spacecraft with a power/toughness box can be your commander (CR 903.12c).
formats.constructed: Same rule (where Spacecraft and Planets are legal, such as Standard).

title: Crewing a Vehicle
answer: Crew N taps any number of your other untapped creatures with total power N or more to make the Vehicle an artifact creature until end of turn. Creatures that just arrived can crew, because crewing isn't their own {T} ability.
coach: Crew with creatures that just came in or wouldn't attack; crewing taps them, so they can't block on the next turn.

formats.commander: Same rule. A legendary Vehicle can be your commander (CR 903.3).
formats.brawl: Same rule. A legendary Vehicle can be your commander (CR 903.12c).

title: Commander damage
answer: A player who has been dealt 21 or more combat damage by the same commander over the game loses. Only combat damage counts, and each commander is tracked separately.
coach: Track commander damage per commander on paper; an evasive commander can win through 21 damage even at high life totals.

formats.commander: Applies: 21 or more combat damage from the same commander makes you lose (CR 903.10a).
formats.brawl: Doesn't apply: Brawl games don't use the commander damage rule (CR 903.12h).
formats.constructed: Doesn't apply: there are no commanders in Standard or other constructed formats.
formats.limited: Doesn't apply in Draft or Sealed. Commander Draft follows the Commander rules, so it does apply there (CR 903.13g).

title: Commander tax
answer: Each time you cast your commander from the command zone, it costs {2} more for each previous time you cast it from there this game.
coach: Before recasting your commander, count the tax; sometimes it's better to protect it than to recast it.

formats.commander: Applies: {2} more for each previous cast from the command zone (CR 903.8).
formats.brawl: Applies: Brawl uses the normal Commander rules, including tax (CR 903.12a).
formats.constructed: Doesn't apply: there are no commanders in Standard or other constructed formats.
formats.limited: Doesn't apply in Draft or Sealed; applies in Commander Draft (CR 903.13g).

title: Where your commander goes
answer: If your commander would go to your hand or library, you may put it into the command zone instead. If it goes to the graveyard or exile, you may move it to the command zone the next time state-based actions are checked (so 'dies' triggers still happen).
coach: Moving your commander to the command zone is optional; leave it in the graveyard if you have recursion that gets it back cheaper.

formats.commander: Applies (CR 903.9a, 903.9b).
formats.brawl: Applies: Brawl uses the normal Commander rules (CR 903.12a).
formats.constructed: Doesn't apply: there's no command zone for commanders in Standard or other constructed formats.
formats.limited: Doesn't apply in Draft or Sealed; applies in Commander Draft (CR 903.13g).

title: Color identity
answer: A card's color identity is every color in its mana cost and rules text (and color indicator). In Commander, every card in your deck must fit within your commander's color identity.
coach: Hybrid and colored symbols in rules text count toward color identity, so check activated abilities before adding a card.

formats.commander: Applies to deck building: every card must fit within your commander's color identity (CR 903.5c), and lands with basic land types only if they make your colors (CR 903.5d).
formats.brawl: Applies, with one exception: if your commander is colorless, you may play any number of basic lands of one basic land type (CR 903.12e).
formats.constructed: Doesn't apply: you can play cards of any colors; only the four-copy limit and the ban list restrict you (CR 100.2a).
formats.limited: Doesn't apply in Draft or Sealed; applies in Commander Draft (CR 903.13f).

title: The legend rule
answer: If you control two or more legendary permanents with the same name, you choose one to keep and put the rest into their owners' graveyards. This is a state-based action.
coach: Copying your own legendary creature makes you sacrifice one, unless the copy says it isn't legendary; plan for the extra 'dies' or 'leaves' triggers.

formats.commander: Same rule. It only checks what each player controls, so several players can each control the same legend.

title: Zero toughness and lethal damage
answer: A creature with 0 or less toughness is put into its owner's graveyard, and regeneration or indestructible can't save it. A creature with lethal damage marked on it is destroyed, which indestructible and regeneration can stop.
coach: Shrinking effects (-X/-X) beat indestructible; save them for indestructible threats.

formats.commander: Same rule.

title: Ordering triggers
answer: When several abilities trigger at once, the active player puts all of theirs on the stack first in any order they choose, then each other player in turn order (APNAP). The last ones put on the stack resolve first.
coach: Order your own triggers so the one that sets things up resolves first; it goes on the stack last.

formats.commander: Same rule. In multiplayer, triggers go on the stack in turn order starting with the active player, so the last player in turn order has theirs resolve first.

title: First strike and double strike
answer: If any attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike, combat has two damage steps. Creatures with first or double strike deal damage in the first step; the others (and double strikers again) in the second.
coach: A first striker can kill a blocker before it deals damage; double strike with a pump spell doubles the bonus.

formats.commander: Same rule. First-strike damage from a commander counts toward 21 commander damage like any combat damage.

title: Hexproof, shroud and ward
answer: Hexproof stops your opponents' spells and abilities from targeting the permanent. Shroud stops everyone, including you. Ward lets them target it, but counters that spell or ability unless they pay the ward cost.
coach: Against ward, make sure you can pay the ward cost before targeting; against hexproof, use board wipes or edicts.

formats.commander: Same rule. Hexproof and ward apply to every opponent, and each opponent who targets a ward permanent has to pay the ward cost.

title: Indestructible
answer: An indestructible permanent can't be destroyed, by lethal damage or 'destroy' effects. It can still be exiled, sacrificed, returned to hand, or put into the graveyard by having 0 or less toughness.
coach: Answer indestructible threats with exile, bounce, edicts or -X/-X effects.

formats.commander: Same rule. An indestructible commander can still be exiled, bounced or sacrificed, and it can then go to the command zone.

title: What a copy copies
answer: A copy copies the original's printed characteristics (plus other copy effects), not its counters, whether it's tapped, attached Auras or Equipment, or other effects changing it. Its 'enters' abilities still trigger.
coach: Copy creatures with strong 'enters' abilities; counters and pump effects on the original won't come along.

formats.commander: Same rule. A copy of a commander isn't a commander: it doesn't deal commander damage and can't go to the command zone.

title: Replacement effects
answer: Effects that say 'instead' (and 'enters with' or 'as … enters') are replacement effects. They change an event as it happens, so they don't use the stack and can't be responded to.
coach: You can't respond to a replacement effect, so plan around it before the event happens.

formats.commander: Same rule. Moving your commander to the command zone instead of your hand or library is itself a replacement effect (CR 903.9b).

title: Poison counters
answer: A player with ten or more poison counters loses the game. This is a state-based action.
coach: Poison counters don't reset; an infect or toxic plan only needs ten total across the game.

formats.commander: Same rule: ten poison counters. (In Two-Headed Giant, a team loses at fifteen; CR 704.6b.)
formats.limited: Same rule: ten poison counters, or fifteen for a team in Two-Headed Giant (CR 704.6b).

title: Mulligans
answer: Draw seven. Each time you mulligan, shuffle and draw seven again, then put one card on the bottom for each mulligan you've taken. In multiplayer games (like Commander), your first mulligan is free.
coach: In multiplayer your first mulligan is free, so mulligan a hand with no lands or no early plays.

formats.commander: Your first mulligan is free in multiplayer games (CR 103.5c). In a two-player Commander game it isn't.
formats.brawl: Your first mulligan is always free, even in a two-player game (CR 903.12g).
formats.constructed: No free mulligan in a two-player game: each mulligan puts one more card on the bottom (CR 103.5).
formats.limited: No free mulligan in a two-player game (CR 103.5); free in multiplayer Limited games such as Two-Headed Giant (CR 103.5c).

title: Cycling
answer: Cycling is an activated ability you use from your hand at instant speed: pay the cost and discard the card to draw a card. The discard is part of the cost, so 'whenever you discard' abilities trigger.
coach: Cycle at the end of an opponent's turn to keep mana open, and to trigger discard payoffs at instant speed.

formats.commander: Same rule.

title: Flash
answer: A card with flash can be cast any time you could cast an instant, including on an opponent's turn and in response to other spells.
coach: Hold flash creatures until the end of an opponent's turn or until they attack, to ambush attackers or dodge sorcery-speed removal.

formats.commander: Same rule. In multiplayer you can cast it on any opponent's turn, such as right before your own turn.

title: Proliferate
answer: To proliferate, choose any number of permanents and players that already have counters, and give each one more of each kind of counter it already has. You can leave out anything you don't want to add to.
coach: Proliferate only what helps you: you can skip your opponents' permanents and players.

formats.commander: Same rule. You can add a poison counter to several opponents at once, or skip any of them.

title: Energy counters
answer: Energy counters ({E}) belong to a player, not a permanent. They stay until you spend them, and paying {E} means removing that many from yourself.
coach: Energy saves between turns, so bank it for a big payoff instead of spending it on small effects.

formats.commander: Same rule.

title: Lifelink
answer: Damage dealt by a source with lifelink makes its controller gain that much life at the same time. It works for any damage, not just combat.
coach: Lifelink works on blocks and noncombat damage too, which can swing a race.

formats.commander: Same rule. Starting life is 40 (CR 903.7).
formats.brawl: Same rule. Starting life is 25 in two-player games and 30 in multiplayer (CR 903.12f).
formats.limited: Same rule. Starting life is 20, or a shared 30 for a Two-Headed Giant team (CR 810.4).

title: Damage wears off
answer: Damage marked on creatures lasts until the cleanup step at the end of the turn, when all damage is removed and 'until end of turn' effects end.
coach: Damage resets every turn, so finish off a damaged creature the same turn with a ping or a second block.

formats.commander: Same rule for damage on creatures. Commander damage dealt to a player is tracked for the whole game and doesn't wear off.

title: Extra combat phases
answer: Effects can add combat phases to a turn; they happen right after the specified phase. An extra combat doesn't come with an extra main phase unless the effect says so.
coach: Make sure your creatures untap or have vigilance before relying on extra combats.

formats.commander: Same rule. In multiplayer you can attack a different opponent in each combat.

title: Menace
answer: A creature with menace can't be blocked except by two or more creatures.
coach: Menace makes chump blocking cost two creatures; pair it with anthems to punish double blocks.

formats.commander: Same rule. In multiplayer only the defending player's creatures can block, so other opponents can't help.

title: Responding and the stack
answer: Yes, in most cases. After a spell is cast or an ability is activated or triggers, players get priority and can respond with instants, flash cards and activated abilities. The last thing added resolves first. You can't respond to playing a land, to mana abilities, or to static or replacement effects.
coach: Wait to respond until the last moment you can; holding priority information keeps opponents guessing.

formats.commander: Same rule. In multiplayer every player gets priority in turn order, and everyone has to pass in a row before anything resolves (CR 117.4).

title: 'Can't' beats 'can'
answer: When one effect says something can happen and another says it can't, the 'can't' effect wins.
coach: 'Can't' effects (like 'can't be countered') beat 'can' effects, so check for them before relying on an interaction.

formats.commander: Same rule.

title: Starting life total
answer: Each player starts with 20 life, unless the format or variant changes it: Commander uses 40.
coach: Higher starting life slows the game down, so Commander rewards long-term engines more than quick aggression.

formats.brawl: 25 life in a two-player game, 30 in multiplayer (CR 903.12f).
formats.limited: 20 life; a Two-Headed Giant team shares 30 (CR 810.4).

title: Deck size and copies
answer: It depends on the format: constructed decks are at least 60 cards with up to four of each card, Limited decks at least 40, and Commander decks exactly 100 singleton cards.
coach: Play the minimum deck size: every extra card makes your best cards less likely to show up.

formats.commander: Exactly 100 cards including your commander, one copy of each card except basic lands, all within the commander's color identity (CR 903.5a–903.5c).
formats.brawl: Exactly 60 cards including your commander, singleton, within its color identity; the commander may also be a planeswalker (CR 903.12c, 903.12d). MTG Arena's Brawl queue uses 100-card decks.
formats.constructed: At least 60 cards, at most four copies of any card except basic lands, and a sideboard of up to 15 cards (CR 100.2a, 100.4a).
formats.limited: At least 40 cards from your own card pool plus basic lands, with as many copies as you opened (CR 100.2b).
